mentally rehearse worst case scenarios to feel prepared

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically as a distraction is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as poorly integrated with the rest of the selected items. The rest of the presentation centers on assault-related fear, hypervigilance, restricted safety, intrusive memories, and alcohol/drug use or mental rehearsal as coping. Physical self-harm introduces a qualitatively different coping pattern that is not supported elsewhere in the triggers, threat, appraisal, or memory items, making the strategy set less coherent.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: 'Lost my connection to my community and culture' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and demographics as presented. The other appraisal items are highly individual and interpersonal ('can't rely on myself', 'permanently an outsider now'), but this item specifically implies a cultural/community rupture that is not otherwise reflected in the triggers, threat items, or other appraisals. Given the provided demographic context, it reads as insufficiently grounded rather than clearly linked to the rest of this sexual-assault formulation.

vignette:
Martha has worked the land her entire life, her hands calloused from decades of planting and harvesting. At sixty-nine, she still put in a full day at the organic farm cooperative, finding a deep satisfaction in the rhythm of the seasons. Eight months ago, that rhythm was shattered. On the last county bus home, with the sun setting over the fields, a man sat beside her. He started with small talk about the dry spell, but his tone shifted, his questions turning personal, his presence becoming heavy and menacing. He was the last one on the bus with her when he moved closer, and in the few minutes before her stop at the end of the long dirt lane to her house, he assaulted her. She stumbled off the bus and into the dusk, the familiar shape of her farmhouse seeming miles away.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of his voice and the rough fabric of his jacket would come to her without warning, vivid and sickening. The rumble of the county bus passing on the main road, a sound she used to ignore, now sent a jolt of raw fear through her. Her heart would pound, and she would immediately feel exposed and unsafe, convinced someone was watching her from the fields. This constant sense of high alert became its own trap; as she scanned the faces of strangers at the feed store, her body already primed for danger, the intense fear would sometimes be enough to pull the memory to the surface, as if her mind was looking for the source of the threat and landing on the original horror.

These intrusive flashes brought with them a crushing weight of self-blame. With the image of his face came the thought, 'I should have screamed. I just sat there. I can't rely on myself.' She began to see herself as fundamentally changed, an outsider to her own life. She would look at her husband, Frank, across the dinner table and feel a chasm between them, certain that he could never understand the foulness that now lived inside her. The more she felt isolated and set apart from him, the more her mind seemed to conjure the past. Sitting alone on the porch while Frank was out, the profound sense of being an outsider would wash over her, and it was in those moments that the memory of the assault would return with its greatest force.

To manage the terror, Martha's world began to shrink. She started by having Frank pick her up from work, unable to bear the thought of the bus. When a neighbour would start a conversation about the local news or some trouble in town, the topic felt too close to the possibility of violence, and Martha would make an excuse and retreat to the house. There, she would pour a glass of whiskey, needing the burn in her throat to quiet the images in her head. But the relief was fleeting; the whiskey she drank to numb herself often had the opposite effect. In the hazy hours after her second glass, the very memories she was trying to suppress would break through with startling clarity, more fragmented and terrifying than when she was sober.

Her self-imposed isolation was reinforced by the belief that she was no longer the person she had been. Convinced she was permanently an outsider, she stopped going to the weekly church social, a staple of her life for forty years. 'They can't understand,' she reasoned, 'I don't belong there anymore.' This conviction made it easier to stay home, where she would mentally rehearse worst-case scenarios-an intruder, a car breaking down-believing that if she could imagine every possible danger, she wouldn't be caught off guard again. This avoidance, however, only made the world outside her property feel more menacing. Her farm became her only safe zone, and the simple act of walking to the mailbox at the end of the lane felt so fraught with peril that she had to constantly look over her shoulder.

Martha finally sought help after her grandson's last visit. He had asked her to walk with him to the end of the lane to wait for his parents, and she found she couldn't do it. The panic was a physical thing, rooting her to the porch steps. Seeing the confusion on his face was more painful than the fear itself. She came to therapy feeling broken, terrified that the damage was permanent. Her deepest hope is not to forget what happened, but to once again feel safe in her own skin, to walk to the end of her lane without looking back.
